tip: 내일 (naeil = tomorrow) never takes 에 (e) – it stands bare. Weekdays do: 토요일에 (toyoire = on Saturday). Yesterday, today and tomorrow all drop the particle.
Korean never fronts question words: 뭐 (mwo = what) sits right where the answer will – 뭐 할 거예요? (mwo hal geoyeyo). The reply slots into the same spot.
저녁 (jeonyeok) means the evening AND the meal you eat then – here 저녁에 (jeonyeoge) = for dinner. One word covers both; context decides.
Clock hours use native Korean numbers: 여덟 시 (yeodeol si = eight o'clock), never Sino 팔 (pal). Minutes switch back to Sino numbers.
살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) is ambiguous: 사다 (sada = buy) and 살다 (salda = live) both shorten to 살. Only context – here 옷을 (oseul = clothes) – says it's 'buy'.
놀다 (nolda) is 'play' with no kid connotation – adults use it too: 친구랑 놀 거예요 (chingurang nol geoyeyo) = I'll hang out with a friend.
English nouns become Korean verbs with 하다 (hada = do): 쇼핑할 거예요 (syopinghal geoyeyo) = will 'do shopping'. Loanwords plug straight in.
(으)로 marks the means: 기차로 (gicharo = by train). There's no word for 'by' – the particle glued onto the noun does the job.
No 'for' with durations – the bare time phrase is enough: 삼 일 있을 거예요 (sam il isseul geoyeyo) = we'll stay three days.
'With' is 랑 (rang) after vowels but 이랑 (irang) after consonants: 부모님이랑 (bumonimirang = with my parents). Casual speech only.
'There will be' is just 있다 (itda = exist): 회의가 있을 거예요 (hoeuiga isseul geoyeyo) = a meeting will exist. No word for 'there'.
바쁘다 (bappeuda = busy) turns straight into 바쁠 거예요 (bappeul geoyeyo = will be busy) – adjectives take the future like verbs, no 'be' needed.
Snow doesn't fall in Korean – it comes: 눈이 올 거예요 (nuni ol geoyeyo = snow will come). Rain uses 오다 (oda = come) too.
You won't find 추울 (chuul) in the dictionary – it's 춥다 (chupda = cold): the ㅂ (b) turns to 우 (u) before endings, giving 추울 거예요 (chuul geoyeyo).
Korean flips 'need': the thing needed is the subject – 우산이 필요할 거예요 (usani piryohal geoyeyo) = 'an umbrella will be necessary', not 'you'll need'.
부터 (buteo = from, starting) glues onto time words: 내일부터 (naeilbuteo = from tomorrow). English puts 'from' before; Korean attaches it after.
동생 (dongsaeng) = any younger sibling, brother or sister – Korean sorts family by age, not gender. Add 여 (yeo) or 남 (nam) only if gender matters.
You call TO someone: 할머니한테 전화할 거예요 (halmeonihante jeonhwahal geoyeyo) – 한테 (hante = to) marks the person, never the object particle 를 (reul).
언니 (eonni = older sister) is what FEMALE speakers say – a man calls his older sister 누나 (nuna). The speaker's gender picks the word.
시 (si) vs 시간 (sigan): 세 시 (se si) = 3 o'clock, but 세 시간 (se sigan) = 3 hours. Adding 간 (gan) turns clock time into a duration.
잘 거예요 (jal geoyeyo) here is 자다 (jada = sleep), not 잘 (jal = well) – they look identical. 'Will sleep' vs 'well': context decides.
씨 (ssi) after a name = polite 'Mr/Ms': 수진 씨 (Sujin ssi). Never attach it to your own name, and never use it alone.
Time 'catches' in Korean: 걸리다 (geollida = to take time, literally 'to hang, catch'). 얼마나 걸릴 거예요? (eolmana geollil geoyeyo) = how long will it take?
